design_detail: Prospective follow-up (a case series) of pregnancies in which a health professional contacted the UK National Teratology Information Service (NTIS) about ecstasy exposure between January 1989 and June 1998: 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up, leaving 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with a known outcome. The enquirer reported the exposure, prescribed and non-prescribed drugs, at the time of the enquiry; the service then contacted the enquirer after the expected delivery date and, where needed, other clinical specialists. There is no unexposed comparison group: the 12 infants with an anomaly among 78 live births are set against external figures (2 to 3% for any anomaly, 5 to 10 per 1000 for heart disease, 1 per 1000 for talipes). A one-page research letter with one table.
can_establish: What was reported to a national teratology service about the outcome of 136 pregnancies exposed to ecstasy, with or without other drugs: 11 miscarriages, 48 elective terminations, 78 live births (66 recorded as normal and 12 with a congenital anomaly), and which anomalies were recorded.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy caused any anomaly: there is no unexposed group; 62 of the 136 mothers also took other drugs; alcohol, smoking, age and illness are not adjusted for; 55% of the enquiries had no known outcome; the anomaly list mixes major findings with minor ones (a toe position, thigh pigmentation, clicking hips); the benchmark percentages are not referenced; no dose or number of tablets is given; anomalies among the 59 miscarried or terminated pregnancies are unknown (no necropsies); nothing is said about development after birth.

sample.recruitment: Enquiries to the NTIS by health professionals, in most cases the patient's general practitioner, about ecstasy exposure in pregnancy, January 1989 to June 1998 (302 enquiries). Follow-up by contacting the enquirer after the expected date of delivery, then other clinical specialists where necessary (Methods paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Pregnancies with a reported ecstasy exposure and a known outcome. Excluded: 31 pregnancies not yet completed (10% of enquiries) and 135 (45%) lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.
sample.demographics: Maternal age at exposure known for 82 women (60%): 26 aged 16 to 20, 31 aged 21 to 25, 20 aged 26 to 31 and five aged 31 to 36. Exposure by trimester: 127 women in the first trimester (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs), two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four women were exposed to several drugs of abuse throughout pregnancy. Acute toxicity from ecstasy was reported in two mothers.
sample.attrition: 55% of enquiries (45% lost, 10% not completed) have no outcome and are not in the analysis; the letter does not compare them with the 136.
sample.selection_effects: Enquiries made by clinicians who were concerned enough to contact a teratology service, so mothers who asked, and clinicians who followed up, are a selected group. The rate of elective termination (35%, 48 of 136) is stated to be higher than the UK average, which suggests that the exposure itself led to terminations; the live-born denominator is therefore selected, and the direction of any resulting bias is unclear.

exposure.measurement: Reported by the enquiring health professional at the time of the enquiry (prescribed and non-prescribed drugs, expected date of delivery); not confirmed by any test; the contents of the tablets are not known.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded in the letter; only the trimester (127 of 136 in the first trimester) and, for the infants with an anomaly, the weeks of exposure (for example 4 weeks, 6 to 12 weeks, first trimester).
exposure.polysubstance: 62 of 136 mothers also took other drugs of abuse (ecstasy and amphetamine 37 women; with cocaine 20; with cannabis 16; with alcohol 13; with LSD 9; with other drugs 13; the counts overlap); four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy; one neonatal death was in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy.

comparison.controls: None. External reference rates are cited without sources: 2 to 3% for congenital anomalies overall; 5 to 10 per 1000 live births for congenital heart disease (24 to 34% of them ventricular septal defects, 7% atrial septal defects); 1 per 1000 for talipes (idiopathic talipes equinovarus has a 3 to 1 male predominance in the UK).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Age is known for 60%; smoking, alcohol quantity, folic acid, other medicines, socio-economic position, illness and family history of malformations are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: None; other drugs are part of the exposure in 62 of 136.

outcomes.instruments: Clinician report to the service after the expected delivery date: miscarriage, termination, live birth, prematurity, birthweight, sex ratio and congenital anomalies (13 findings in the table: 12 in live-born infants and one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs).
outcomes.validity_norms: No definition of congenital anomaly, no coding system and no examination protocol are given; the table includes minor findings (left fourth toe lying under the third, right-sided plagiocephaly, pigmentation of the right thigh, ptosis, clicking hips) alongside major ones (ventricular septal defects, hydrocephalus, absent upper limbs).
outcomes.operationalization: Proportion of live births with an anomaly, with a 95% confidence interval (the editors reproduce the intervals by an exact binomial method to within 0.1 percentage point), compared informally with the external figures; subgroup rates for heart and 'musculoskeletal' anomalies.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the subgroups (heart disease, talipes) were chosen after the table was drawn up.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; whoever reported the outcome knew of the exposure.

analysis.effect_sizes: 12 of 78 live-born infants had an anomaly: 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4; the editors' exact interval is 8.2 to 25.3) against an expected 2 to 3%. Two infants had congenital heart disease (ventricular septal defects): 26 per 1000 live births (CI 3.0 to 90.0) against 5 to 10 per 1000. Three infants (all girls) had talipes: 38 per 1000 (CI 8 to 109) against 1 per 1000; this is also the figure the abstract gives as 'musculoskeletal anomalies'. Miscarriage 11 of 136 (8%, within the expected range); elective termination 48 (35%); 8 premature births (25 to 36 weeks, including twins born at 25 weeks); one neonatal death; only three infants under 2.5 kg among those born at term; no effect on sex ratio. By the editors' reading of the table, the three infants with talipes were in the ecstasy-only group, and both infants with a ventricular septal defect had other drug exposure (amphetamine and gamma hydroxybutyric acid in one, alcohol in the other).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A service database, not a registered study; an interim report of 92 pregnancies was published as an abstract in 1998 (cited).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract highlights heart and 'musculoskeletal' anomalies, which rest on 2 and 3 infants and were chosen from the 13 findings in the table; the 'musculoskeletal' rate equals the talipes count and the letter does not say which other findings were counted under it.
analysis.power: No calculation; the authors state that the series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 78 live-born infants whose mothers reported ecstasy in pregnancy, 12 (15.4%) had a recorded anomaly, a higher proportion than the 2 to 3% the authors cite, but the comparison is with an unreferenced benchmark of uncertain definition, in a group where 55% of enquiries had no outcome, 62 of 136 mothers took other drugs and the list mixes minor with major findings. Two infants had heart defects (both with other drug exposure) and three had talipes. The numbers are too small and the comparison too uncontrolled to say whether ecstasy changes the chance of an anomaly.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the drug may be associated with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects (15.4%), with heart and musculoskeletal anomalies predominant; the text calls the data important while stating that the series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly.

timeline.event: Interim report of 92 pregnancies from the same service, published as a conference abstract (cited in this letter; not read)
Dutch teratology service reported 43 pregnancies after ecstasy exposure (cited in this letter; not read); the authors know of one other case of congenital heart disease from it

Prospective cohort of 96 women recruited in pregnancy (28 exposed to MDMA) that compares infant development, not anomalies; its Introduction describes this letter as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies, neither of which the letter prints (its Discussion's 15.4% 'increased risk' echoes the letter's own summary)

replication.where_it_stands: No study read here has repeated a count of congenital anomalies after MDMA with a comparison group. The 2012 cohort studied development at 1 and 4 months instead; one of its 28 exposed infants had a rare genetic syndrome that its authors attribute to a spontaneous mutation.

funding.funder: No funding statement; the letter thanks the patients, the Drug Information pharmacists, health-care personnel and a statistician.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: the letter carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors work at the National Teratology Information Service (Regional Drug and Therapeutics Centre, Newcastle) and the Scottish Poisons Information Bureau; the service that collected the data is the authors' own.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort or registry with an unexposed comparison group matched or adjusted for age, smoking, alcohol, other drugs and illness; enrolment in early pregnancy with few lost to follow-up; a stated definition of major anomalies using a standard coding system; exposure timing and amount from interview and, where possible, biological confirmation; and enough exposed pregnancies (hundreds) to give usable intervals for heart and limb defects.

domains.note: No comparison group at all; 62 of 136 mothers also took other drugs; alcohol, smoking, age, illness and folate are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Only enquiries to a service, and only those with a known outcome (136 of 302); 35% of the pregnancies were terminated.
Exposure is reported second-hand by the enquirer, without confirmation, dose or tablet contents.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not applicable: the exposure was not assigned; other drugs are counted under confounding.
45% of enquiries were lost to follow-up and 10% not completed; no outcomes for those pregnancies, and no necropsy data for the 59 miscarried or terminated ones.
Anomalies were reported by whoever enquired, with no definition or coding, no systematic examination, and knowledge of the exposure; minor findings are included.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The abstract's headline is a crude comparison with an unreferenced benchmark; the heart and 'musculoskeletal' subgroups rest on 2 and 3 infants and were chosen after the table was drawn up.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A case series without an unexposed comparison group, from enquiries to a service, with 55% of enquiries lacking an outcome, other drugs in nearly half the exposures and an undefined anomaly list: it cannot show whether ecstasy changes the chance of an anomaly. The source can be cited for what was reported to the service (136 pregnancies, 78 live births, 12 recorded anomalies and which), with its limits stated; it cannot be cited for a risk, a risk ratio, or any statement that ecstasy causes or does not cause anomalies.

key_findings.finding: The UK National Teratology Information Service followed up 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with ecstasy exposure from January 1989 to June 1998; there were 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 3rd paragraph (opens 'The UK National Teratology Information Service'; the boxed summary counts as the 1st paragraph)

key_findings.finding: The enquirer was asked for drug exposure, prescribed and non-prescribed, at the time of the enquiry and the expected delivery date; follow-up was by contacting the enquirer after the expected date of delivery and, where necessary, other clinical specialists.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 4th paragraph (opens 'In each case the enquirer was asked')

key_findings.finding: 74 women reported ecstasy only and 62 ecstasy with other drugs of abuse (amphetamine 37, cocaine 20, cannabis 16, alcohol 13, LSD 9, other 13); acute toxicity from ecstasy in two mothers; maternal age known for 82 (60%): 26 aged 16 to 20, 31 aged 21 to 25, 20 aged 26 to 31, five aged 31 to 36.

127 women (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs) were exposed in the first trimester, two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy.

11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage (8%, within the expected range) and 48 in elective termination (35%, higher than the UK average; one after prenatal diagnosis of malformations); no necropsy data on the other aborted fetuses.

78 live-born infants: 66 normal and 12 with congenital anomalies, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), described as significantly higher than an expected incidence of 2 to 3%; the table lists 13 anomaly findings (12 live-born, plus one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs), in groups by drug exposure: ecstasy alone 7 rows, ecstasy with amphetamine and gamma hydroxybutyric acid 1, with alcohol 3 and with amphetamine 2.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 8th paragraph (opens 'There were 78 liveborn infants'); Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)

key_findings.finding: Eight infants were born prematurely (25 to 36 weeks, including twins at 25 weeks; two fetal distress cases thought unrelated to ecstasy); one neonatal death in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy; no adverse effect on sex ratio; birthweights within the expected range for term infants with only three under 2.5 kg.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 9th and 10th paragraphs (open 'Eight infants were born prematurely' and 'No adverse effects were observed in the sex ratio')

key_findings.finding: Three female infants had talipes (38 per 1000, CI 8 to 109, against an expected 1 per 1000; idiopathic talipes equinovarus is male-predominant 3 to 1 in the UK); two infants had congenital heart disease, ventricular septal defects (26 per 1000, CI 3.0 to 90.0, against an expected 5 to 10 per 1000); the authors say the small series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly but consider the data important.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 11th and 12th paragraphs (open 'There were three female infants with talipes' and 'The spontaneous incidence of congenital heart disease'); abstract

reporting_issues.issue: The 15.4% is called significantly higher than an 'expected incidence of 2-3%', with no source or definition for the benchmark; the 12 live-born infants with an anomaly include minor findings (left fourth toe under the third, right-sided plagiocephaly, pigmentation of the right thigh, ptosis of the left eye, clicking hips) as well as major ones.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison is not like with like: a benchmark for major malformations set against a list of mixed severity. The proportion cannot be read as a risk or a risk ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: Of 302 enquiries, 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up and 31 (10%) not completed; the letter does not compare them with the 136 followed.
reporting_issues.consequence: If outcomes were reported back more often when something was wrong, or when the baby was well, the proportion would be biased in either direction; the size of the bias is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Elective terminations were 35% (48 of 136) and 11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage; no necropsy data exist for the other aborted fetuses (one fetus had absent upper limbs and was terminated).
reporting_issues.consequence: Anomalies in 59 non-live pregnancies are largely unknown, and the live-born denominator may be selected; the table's count of 12 refers to live births only.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's rate for 'musculoskeletal anomalies' (38 per 1000) is the same figure the text gives for talipes alone (3 infants); the letter does not say which other findings (toe position, clinodactyly, clicking hips) were counted under it, and the abstract's 'cardiovascular' rate rests on 2 infants, both of whom were also exposed to other drugs (amphetamine and gamma hydroxybutyric acid in one, alcohol in the other) by the table's grouping.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup rates have very wide intervals (3 to 90 and 8 to 109 per 1000) and cannot be attributed to ecstasy alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The expected rate of talipes (1 per 1000) is set against three girls, although the letter says idiopathic talipes is male-predominant 3 to 1; the rate is not tested and the unusual sex distribution is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three cases cannot establish an excess; the sex pattern is noted by the authors but not interpreted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract speaks of 136 'babies' exposed; there were 136 pregnancies, of which 78 ended in live births (one pair of twins counts as two).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 136 pregnancies and 78 live births; the 15.4% has a denominator of 78.

reporting_issues.issue: A later paper (Singer et al., 2012) describes this letter in its Introduction as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the letter contains no risk ratio, no adjusted analysis and no such multiples (15.4% is a proportion, which the authors compare informally with 2 to 3%, a ratio of about 5 to 8 by the editors' arithmetic). The 2012 paper's Discussion wording, a 15.4% 'increased risk', echoes the letter's own summary.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 4 to 7 times and two-fold figures should not be quoted from the 2012 paper as findings of this letter.

verification.source_read: PDF McElhatton_1999_CongenitalAnomalies.pdf (2 pages, Lancet 354:1441-1442; the letter and its table are on p. 1441, read as text and on a rendered page; the rest of the PDF is an unrelated letter on tonsillar cancer). Supplementary material: none.
